source_text: et quomodo disserat alvi naturam stomacho esse subiectam, quod cibi et potionis sit, receptaculum: pulmones autem et cor extrinsecus spiritum adducant; multa in alvo mirabiliter effecta, quae constarent ex nervis; et quod sit multiplex et tortuosa, arceatque et contineat, sive illud aridum sit, sive humidum quod receperit Balbus apud Tullium cum Cotta vere diligenterque disseruit . Unde ob hoc pauca ponis - ut dicis - ut oneres pudorem meum, non ea me intellexisse sub magisterio sacrae legis, ad quorum notionem Gentiles solo rationis ductu pervenire potuerunt quemadmodum reliquiae cibi depellantur, tum astringentibus se intestinis, tum relaxantibus
pass_a_gloss: And how disserat alvi nature stomacho to-be subiectam, that/which cibi and potionis may-be, receptaculum: pulmones however and heart extrinsecus Spirit adducant; many-things in alvo mirabiliter effecta, which constarent from nervis; and that/which may-be multiplex and tortuosa, arceatque and contineat, or that aridum may-be, or humidum that/which receperit Balbus before Tullium when/with Cotta truly diligenterque disseruit. whence on-account-of this few-things ponis - so-that/as you-say - so-that/as oneres modesty my, not she/it me intellexisse under magisterio sacrae of-the-law, to quorum notionem Gentiles solo of-reason ductu pervenire potuerunt just-as reliquiae cibi depellantur, then astringentibus himself intestinis, then relaxantibus.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Balbus, in Cicero, discussed the matter truthfully and carefully with Cotta.
[I quote] a few things to increase his shame: under the teaching of the sacred law he has failed to understand things that pagans could grasp through reason alone.
[Balbus] touches on the working of the sexes under the subject of animals because, for the sake of propriety, he passed over it in describing human beings.

[He] portrays the human being in words: the stomach lies below the gullet as a receptacle for food and drink; the lungs and heart draw breath from outside; many things in the stomach are wonderfully fashioned from sinews; its many folds and windings hold and contain what it receives, whether dry or liquid.
[The remaining food is expelled] as the intestines alternately contract and relax.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
